sections.html:
The Terrebonne Parish Assessor values property, and the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's tax office collects the bill. The Assessor's office is in the Government Tower in Houma and is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. The Tax Collector's office handles payment of tax bills.

Office or ruleDetail
Assessor phone985-876-6620
Tax Collector phone985-857-0230
HoursMonday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Tax due date (state rule)December 31
Interest on unpaid tax (state rule)1% per month
Homestead exemption (state rule)$7,500 assessed value, $75,000 market value

Your house is taxed on 10% of what it would sell for, and the state orders a fresh reassessment at least once every four years. Each taxing body then applies its own millage rate to that assessed figure. A mill is $1 for each $1,000 of assessed value, which makes a 20-mill levy $20 per $1,000.

Louisiana tax bills combine levies from several taxing bodies, and which ones appear depends on the address. A house inside Houma and one on a bayou road can carry different totals. The Assessor and the Tax Collector can tell you which levies apply to yours.

  • Check the parcel record for the taxing districts listed.
  • Compare last year's bill with this year's assessed value.
  • Ask the Tax Collector about any special districts that apply.

Use the public inspection period to look over your assessment. If the number seems wrong, take it to the local Board of Review. The inspection period is usually August 15 to September 15.

  • Pull your parcel record and check the facts on it.
  • Collect evidence such as a recent appraisal, damage photos or repair estimates.
  • Contact the Assessor before the Board of Review deadline, which varies by year.

An owner who loses at the Board of Review can go on to the Louisiana Tax Commission and then to court. Damaged houses give owners the strongest cases, which makes a Hurricane Ida repair file worth keeping.

sections.h2: When tax is due and what if you miss it
sections.html:
The bill arrives by mail in December and must be paid by the 31st. Every month after that adds 1% interest.

A balance that stays open can end with the property sold at a tax sale. The owner then gets three years to redeem it. Think of that as a last-resort cushion, since costs and interest grow all the while.

If you are selling, closing takes care of the balance out of your proceeds. Ask the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230 for a payoff letter so the title company has an exact figure.

sections.h2: Reading your bill, step by step
sections.html:
A Terrebonne bill looks dense, but five checks cover most questions.

  1. Confirm the owner name and the parcel description match your deed.
  2. Find the assessed value, which should be about a tenth of fair market value.
  3. Look for the homestead exemption. It takes $7,500 off the assessed value if you own and live in the house.
  4. List the taxing districts. A house inside Houma may show levies that a bayou road address does not.
  5. Note the due date, December 31, and the interest that starts afterward.

Keep a copy of every bill you pay, since a receipt settles most disputes about whether a year was covered. If something looks off, call the Assessor at 985-876-6620 for value questions and the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230 for payment questions. They are separate offices, and each can only fix its own part.

A buyer's title company will pull the same record, so errors that you fix now do not become surprises at closing.

Rain here runs about 65 inches a year, mostly from June through September, and Houma sits about 10 feet above sea level. Low ground and heavy rain make flood questions part of nearly every sale. Check where your parcel falls on the current FEMA flood map before you list, because buyers and insurers will.

On August 29, 2021, Hurricane Ida struck as a Category 4 storm, with 150 mph winds at landfall near Port Fourchon, and it damaged or destroyed many houses in Houma. Francine followed, coming ashore in the parish on September 11, 2024. Buyers of houses from that stretch ask what was fixed and who did the work, so pull together your repair files and insurance claims early.

The parish had 109,580 people in the 2020 census and an estimated 104,163 in 2025, with 33,406 of them in Houma. Bayou Cane is the largest unincorporated area next to the city.

sections.h2: What to gather before selling with tax due
sections.html:
Four documents make a sale move: a tax payoff, the parcel record, your deed and any storm repair papers. With them in hand, a buyer or title company can get to work right away. Here is where each one comes from.

  • Tax payoff or bill: the Tax Collector, 985-857-0230.
  • Assessment and parcel record: the Assessor, 985-876-6620.
  • Recorded deed and mortgage history: the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court.
  • Flood zone status: the current FEMA flood map for the parish.

If you are behind on tax and the house is also in poor repair, say so up front. A buyer who knows the full picture can set a price and a timeline that account for it.

A conventional sale asks the house to pass an appraisal and the buyer's inspection, and lenders often refuse to fund a house with open storm damage. A cash buyer does not need that approval, which is why cash is common for damaged Terrebonne houses.

It does not skip the public records. The title company still searches the Clerk of Court's records, confirms the tax status with the Tax Collector and records the new deed. Your part is to have the payoff, the parcel record, your deed and the repair papers ready.

Compare any cash price with what listing would leave you after repairs, carrying costs and commissions, then decide.

sections.h2: Selling a storm-damaged house with tax owed
sections.html:
Plenty of Terrebonne owners are dealing with a tax balance and a storm-battered house at once. Selling as-is for cash can solve both. The buyer takes on the repairs, and the title company settles the tax out of the proceeds.

  • Get your tax payoff in writing.
  • Collect roof and repair records from Ida or Francine.
  • Check flood zone status on the current FEMA map.
  • Record the sale with the Terrebonne Clerk of Court after closing.

The deed must name who is responsible for property taxes, so the buyer's bill goes to the right address next December.

Expect the title company to ask for the payoff first. Once it has a number, it can schedule the act of sale, pay the balance from your proceeds and send the rest to you. Handing it the parcel record and your deed on day one saves a round of phone calls. Heirs and owners who live out of state can do all of this by phone and email, since the Assessor, the Tax Collector and the Clerk of Court each take requests without a visit.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Terrebonne Parish?
faqs.a: The Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's tax office collects it. You can reach the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230.

faqs.q: When is Terrebonne Parish property tax due?
faqs.a: State rules set the due date at December 31. Interest of 1% per month starts after that.

faqs.q: What is the homestead exemption in Terrebonne Parish?
faqs.a: For an owner-occupied home, it takes $7,500 off the assessed value. That equals $75,000 of fair market value.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Terrebonne Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Review it during the roll inspection period and then appeal to the Board of Review. The inspection window is usually August 15 to September 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a hurricane-damaged house in Terrebonne Parish?
faqs.a: Yes. An as-is sale works, and any unpaid tax is paid out of the proceeds when you close.
